1.title: Find the authenticity and resale problem
1.intro: Fashion has problems with fakes, hidden labour and waste. A shared digital record can tie a garment to its origin, owner history and repair record.
pts: List buyer worries: fake goods, unknown origin, resale value, repair history.
Choose one product: a bag, a jacket or a pair of shoes, and a first brand partner.
Decide the record: material source, maker, date, size, care and each change of owner.
Test the need with ten shoppers: would proof of origin change what you pay?
Interview one repair shop and one resale seller to learn what proof of origin they need most and what they check today.
Write the buyer's questions as a list (Is it real? Where was it made? Who owned it? Was it repaired?) and match each to a field in the record.
Choose the first line by picking an item with a high price, frequent copying or a resale market, and count how many units exist.
1.ex: Assume (teaching figures, not market facts) that a resale buyer pays 15% more for a bag with a verified history and a repair record, and that fakes cost the brand 2% of sales. If the bag normally resells for 400, 15% more is 400 x 0.15 = 60, so 460. If the brand sells 500,000 a year, 2% lost to fakes is 10,000.
1.act: Survey ten shoppers and one brand and write the problem in one page.
1.std: Survey shows a real willingness to pay.

2.title: Know consumer, textile and data rules
2.intro: Fashion claims and labels are regulated, so check each rule before you launch.
pts: Federal textile labelling rules require fibre content to be shown in English and French; care labels are voluntary but any care claim must be true. Check the current rule for your product.
Claims such as 'sustainable' or 'ethical' must be provable under competition law.
Customer personal data is protected by privacy law and should not sit on a record that cannot be erased.
Cross-border sales add customs, duty and product-safety rules.
Check which country-of-origin wording you may use on a label, and keep supplier records that back it up.
Ask a privacy adviser whether a tag linked to an owner needs consent and how a person can delete their data; collect only what is needed.
List which claims go on the tag, the website and ads, and who approves each claim before it is published.
2.ex: Row: 'Claim recycled content | competition law and labelling rules | hold supplier certificate | before launch | certificate on file'. Second row: 'Label a jacket for sale in Canada | federal textile labelling rules | check the fibre content label in both languages and the care label if you add one | before launch | label proof approved'. Check the provincial rule for any extra requirements.
2.act: Build a rules table for one product line.

3.title: Design the digital product passport
3.intro: Keep the record small and useful.
pts: Attach a tag: QR code, NFC chip or hidden label that cannot be copied easily.
Record business facts only: lot, maker, date, material, certificate numbers.
Let owners add care and repair entries; a transfer is a new entry.
Test the tag after washing, rubbing and sunlight.
Test ten tags each for rubbing, folding, rain and sunlight, and tabulate scan success for each test.
Choose where the tag sits: hidden, protected and easy to scan, and photograph the spot for the guide.
Build a scan page that shows only business facts and a plain message if the tag is unknown or already used.
3.ex: After 20 washes, 18 of 20 QR labels still scanned and 2 failed. Survival is 18 / 20 = 90%. That passes the 50% stop rule, but a 10% failure rate is too high for a lasting record, so test a woven label next.
3.act: Prototype a passport for one garment and test the tag.

4.title: Price the service and prove the gain
4.intro: Brands pay when the passport raises sales or cuts fakes.
pts: Charge the brand a fee per item tagged; the worked example below uses 1.80 per item.
List the brand's gains: price premium, resale royalty, fewer fakes and better returns data.
List your own costs: tags, hosting, support and onboarding.
Work out break-even volume as fixed cost divided by margin per item.
Estimate the price premium the brand can charge, and the share of it the passport must earn to be worth the fee.
Compare tag types (QR label, woven label, NFC chip) and check that your choice fits within the 0.60 variable cost.
Quote a pilot package: setup fee, per-item fee and a review at day 90.
4.ex: Fee 1.80 per item; variable cost 0.60; margin 1.20; fixed cost 8,000 a month needs about 6,700 items a month. Teaching figures in CAD. Check: 6,700 x 1.20 = 8,040, just above 8,000. At 50% volume, 3,350 items give 3,350 x 1.20 = 4,020, leaving a monthly gap of 8,000 - 4,020 = 3,980.
4.act: Build the model with a 50% volume case.

5.title: Run supplier onboarding and data quality
pts: Train suppliers to scan at each step.
Verify supplier entries with audits and photos.
Tell the supplier what went wrong as soon as an audit finds an error.
Track the share of items with a complete record each week.
Give each supplier a one-page checklist: what to scan, when, and whom to call if the tag does not work.
Audit a sample of 20 records a week against photos and paper documents, and record the error rate.
Never delete an entry; add a correction with date, reason and who made it.
5.ex: Pilot: 85% of items had a complete record after 6 weeks. Of 2,000 items tagged, 85% complete means 1,700 full records and 300 incomplete. A target of 95% is 1,900, so 200 more records must be completed.

6.title: Sell to brands and marketplaces
6.intro: Start with a brand that has a fake or resale problem.
pts: Offer a 90-day pilot on one line.
Show a live scan demo to every brand you meet.
Partner with repair shops and resale sites.
Track the funnel from brands contacted to demos to pilots.
Prepare a three-minute live demo: scan a tag, show the history, and add a repair entry.
Meet a repair shop and a resale seller, agree how they will add entries, and record their needs.
Write a one-page pilot offer: line, units, fee, dates, measures and exit terms.
6.ex: Funnel: 20 brands, 6 demos, 2 pilots. Brand to demo is 6 / 20 = 30%, demo to pilot is 2 / 6 = 33%, and overall 2 / 20 = 10%. At 10%, winning 5 pilots needs about 50 brands.

7.title: Manage greenwashing, privacy and tech risks
7.intro: A record can mislead if inputs are wrong.
pts: Claim only what you can prove.
Keep personal data off the shared record.
Plan for tag failure and re-tagging.
Prepare for the brand leaving the service.
Keep a claims log: each public claim, its evidence, the date checked and the person who signed it off.
Design the tag to carry only an item number, with all other data held in a record you can correct and delete.
Write a brand-exit plan: how owners keep access to history if the brand stops using the service, and how data is exported.
7.ex: Risk: 'Wrong origin entered | 3 x 5 | audit and photo proof | quality lead | monthly'. The score is 3 x 5 = 15 out of 25, so it is high priority. After audits with photo proof, likelihood falls to 2 and the score is 2 x 5 = 10.

8.title: Pilot and scale
pts: Run the pilot for 90 days on one product line.
Measure scan rate, resale uplift, fakes found.
Stop rule: under 50% tag survival means change tag.
Decide at day 90 whether to proceed, change the tag or stop.
Record three numbers each week: scan rate, tags lost and fakes found, and plot each.
Collect resale prices for tagged and untagged items of the same type and compare the averages.
Plan a second line only after the review, and list what must be fixed first.
8.ex: Tag survival 94%; resale uplift 12%. Of 500 tagged items, 94% is 470 tags still scanning at day 90, far above the 50% stop rule. A 12% resale uplift on a 400 bag is 400 x 0.12 = 48; decision: proceed.

quiz: What does a product passport record?
Business facts such as lot, maker, date, material and certificates.
How is an ownership change recorded?
As a new entry.
Why keep personal data off the record?
It cannot easily be erased.
Why test tags after washing?
Tags must survive real use.
Which rules require "sustainable" claims to be provable?
Competition and labelling rules; check the current federal and provincial rule.
What is break-even?
Fixed cost divided by margin per item.
Why audit suppliers?
Inputs decide whether the record is true.
Name two brand gains.
Price premium and fewer fakes (or resale royalty).
What triggers a tag change?
Under 50% tag survival.
Why use English and French labels?
Fibre content labelling under federal textile rules generally needs both languages; check the rule for your product.
